title: Of means times, and find the rule
summary: Take a fraction or mixed number of an amount, then find the rule hiding inside a pattern.

problems.prompt: About how many leaves are on a big oak tree?
explanation: Guess and round: estimate with easy numbers first, one part at a time.
A big tree has about 20 large branches, round it to 20.
Each large branch has about 100 smaller twigs, round it to 100.
Each twig holds about 100 leaves, round it to 100.
20 x 100 x 100 is 200,000, so about 200,000 leaves is the closest guess.
problems.useAgain: when a real count is too big to do one at a time, so you break it into easy parts and multiply.
hints: Do not try to count leaves one at a time. Break the tree into branches, twigs, and leaves per twig.
Multiply the three easy round numbers together to get your estimate.
problems.socraticHint: A tree isn't one thing to count, it's branches of twigs of leaves. What would happen to your final estimate if you were a little off on each of those three guesses?

variant.prompt: About how many needles are on a large pine tree?

problems.prompt: About how many minutes are there in a year?
explanation: Guess and round: a day has 24 hours times 60 minutes, which is close to 1,500 minutes when you round up a little.
A year has about 365 days. Round that down to 350, a friendlier number to multiply.
1,500 x 350 is 525,000, so about 500,000 minutes is the closest guess.
problems.useAgain: when you need minutes, seconds or some other tiny unit spread across a much bigger stretch of time.
hints: Think about how many minutes are in one day first.
Multiply the minutes in a day by the days in a year, using round numbers for both.
problems.socraticHint: A year is a long stretch made of many short minutes. Which feels easier to be confident about: the minutes in one day, or the number of days in a year?

variant.prompt: About how many seconds are there in a week?

problems.prompt: About how many times does your heart beat in one day?
explanation: Guess and round: your heart beats about 70 times a minute, round that up to 100 beats a minute.
There are about 1,440 minutes in a day, round that down to 1,000 minutes.
100 x 1,000 is 100,000, so about 100,000 beats is the closest guess.
problems.useAgain: when something repeats at a steady rate and you need a total over a whole day.
hints: Think about how many times your heart beats in one minute.
Multiply the beats per minute by the number of minutes in a day.
problems.socraticHint: Your heart keeps the same steady beat whether you are asleep or running around. Does that make a whole day's total easier or harder to estimate than you first thought?

variant.prompt: About how many times does your heart beat in one week?

problems.prompt: A movie theater sells out every seat for all showings in one day, every day it is open. About how many total tickets does it sell in one year?
explanation: Guess and round: break it into seats, showings and days, one part at a time.
A theater might seat about 200 people, and run about 5 showings a day: 200 x 5 is 1,000 tickets a day.
A year has about 350 selling days, so 1,000 x 350 is 350,000 tickets a year.
problems.useAgain: when a yearly total is built from three multiplying parts instead of two, like seats, showings and days.
hints: Break the year down into seats per showing, showings per day, and days per year, not all at once.
Multiply the three rounded numbers together in any order.
problems.socraticHint: If you were off by a little on the seats-per-theater guess, would that change your final answer's first digit, or just its last couple of zeros?

variant.prompt: A small stadium sells out every game for a whole season. About how many total tickets does it sell in one season?

problems.prompt: About how many total hours of sleep does a kid get from birth to age 10?
explanation: Guess and round: a kid sleeps about 10 hours a night, round the year to 350 nights.
10 x 350 is 3,500 hours in one year.
Over about 10 years, 3,500 x 10 is 35,000 hours total.
problems.useAgain: when a total stretches over several years, and you need to multiply a yearly estimate by the number of years too.
hints: Find one year's worth of sleep hours first, before multiplying by the number of years.
Round hours per night and nights per year to easy numbers before multiplying.
problems.socraticHint: Once you know roughly how many hours a kid sleeps in one year, what is the very last multiplication left to do?

variant.prompt: About how many total hours of sleep does a kid get from birth to age 5?

problems.prompt: About how many gallons of water does a family of four use in one year, if each person uses about 80 gallons a day?
explanation: Guess and round: one person uses about 80 gallons a day, so four people use about 320 gallons a day.
A year has about 350 days worth counting, so 320 x 350 is the yearly total.
320 x 350 is 112,000 gallons for the whole family in a year.
problems.useAgain: when a daily rate for one person needs to scale up by both the number of people and the number of days.
hints: Find the family's daily total before you multiply by days in a year.
320 x 350 is the same as 32 x 35 with three zeros added back on.
problems.socraticHint: Which changes your answer more: being a little off on gallons per person, or being a little off on days in a year?

variant.prompt: About how many gallons of water does a family of five use in one year, if each person uses about 70 gallons a day?

problems.prompt: Your LED circuit from week 3 uses about 3 thousandths of an amp when lit. About how many thousandths of an amp would 5 of these circuits use, all lit at once? Now if you added 5 more circuits just like that, about how many thousandths of an amp would all 10 use together?
explanation: Current is a flow: 3 thousandths of an amp is the flow through one circuit.
5 circuits lit together add their flows: 3 times 5 is 15 thousandths of an amp.
10 circuits is double 5, so double 15: that gives 30 thousandths of an amp.
problems.useAgain: when several circuits share the same current draw and you need the total flow for all of them.
hints: Find the flow for 5 circuits first, before jumping to 10.
10 circuits is exactly double 5 circuits, so double your first answer.
problems.socraticHint: If one circuit needs 3 thousandths of an amp, does doubling the number of circuits double the total flow too?

variant.prompt: Your LED circuit uses about 4 thousandths of an amp when lit. About how many thousandths of an amp would 5 of these circuits use, all lit at once? Now if you added 5 more circuits just like that, about how many thousandths of an amp would all 10 use together?

problem.prompt: A stack of unit cubes sits on a table, built in three layers, one directly on top of the next. The bottom layer is a full rectangle of cubes, 4 wide and 3 deep, with no gaps. The middle layer sits exactly on top of the bottom layer and is also a full 4 by 3 rectangle, with no gaps. The top layer sits on top of the middle layer, but it only covers a 2 by 3 patch in the back corner. How many cubes are in the whole stack, including the ones hidden underneath and inside?
explanation: Count the hidden ones too, layer by layer, since most of this stack is hidden underneath the top.
The bottom layer is 4 by 3, so it has 12 cubes.
The middle layer sits exactly on the bottom layer and is also 4 by 3, so it adds 12 more cubes.
The top layer only covers part of the middle layer, a 2 by 3 patch, so it adds 6 more cubes.
12 plus 12 plus 6 is 30 cubes in total, even though you can only see the top layer and the outside faces.
problem.useAgain: when a stack, box or building hides most of its pieces underneath or inside the parts you can actually see.
hints: Work out how many cubes are in each layer separately before adding them up.
The bottom two layers are full rectangles hidden under the layer above; do not forget to count them.
problem.socraticHint: Which of the three layers can you actually see completely from outside the stack, and which ones are you just trusting are still under there?

figure.alt: Three layer footprints, bottom to top: a full 4 by 3 bottom layer, a full 4 by 3 middle layer, and a top layer that only fills a 2 by 3 patch in one back corner of its own 4 by 3 outline.

variant.prompt: A stack of unit cubes sits on a table, built in two layers, one directly on top of the other. The bottom layer is a full rectangle of cubes, 3 wide and 3 deep, with no gaps. The top layer sits exactly on top of the bottom layer, but it only covers a 3 by 2 patch at the front. How many cubes are in the whole stack, including the ones hidden underneath?

figure.alt: Two layer footprints: a full 3 by 3 bottom layer, and a top layer that only fills a 3 by 2 patch at the front of its own 3 by 3 outline.

steps.title: Fractions of quantities and mixed numbers

explanationFigure.alt: Two bars, each cut into 12 equal pieces. The first bar has 8 shaded for 2 thirds, the second bar has 9 shaded for 3 quarters, the two fractions chained together in this problem.

problems.prompt: Suppose a resistor is rated at 330 ohms. You want a new resistor rated at 3/4 of 2/3 of that value. What is the new resistor's rating, in ohms?
explanation: Of means times: 'of' is a hidden multiplication sign, and you can chain more than one 'of' in a row.
First find 2/3 of 330: divide by 3 to get 110, then multiply by 2 to get 220.
Now find 3/4 of that 220: divide by 4 to get 55, then multiply by 3 to get 165 ohms.
problems.useAgain: when a problem chains two 'of' fractions in a row, one applied to the result of the other.
hints: Turn each 'of' into a multiplication sign, one at a time, in order.
Work out the first fraction of 330 completely before you take a fraction of that result.
problems.socraticHint: Does it matter which of the two fractions, 2/3 or 3/4, you apply to 330 first, or would multiplying them together first give the same final answer?

variant.prompt: Suppose a resistor rated at 330 ohms is replaced by one rated at 1/2 of 4/5 of that value. What is the new resistor's rating, in ohms?

explanationFigure.alt: A grid of 5 rows and 8 columns, 40 squares total, with a 4 by 5 block of 20 squares shaded in the corner, showing that 5 eighths of 4 fifths is 20 out of 40, or 1 half of the original charge.

problems.prompt: A robot's battery holds 4/5 of its charge after a long run. Of that remaining charge, 3/8 is used for the trip home, leaving the rest. What fraction of the ORIGINAL full charge is left after the trip home?
explanation: Of means times: 3/8 of the remaining 4/5 charge is used, leaving 5/8 of that remaining charge.
5/8 of 4/5 is (5x4)/(8x5), which simplifies before multiplying: the 5s cancel, leaving 4/8, which is 1/2.
So half of the ORIGINAL full charge is left after the trip home.
problems.useAgain: when a fraction of a fraction of the original amount is left, after some has already been used twice.
hints: Work out what fraction is LEFT of the remaining charge before multiplying, not what fraction is used.
Multiply the two fractions of the original amount straight across, then simplify.
problems.socraticHint: Is finding what fraction is left after using 3/8 the same question as finding what fraction was used?

variant.prompt: A robot's battery holds 9/10 of its charge after a long run. Of that remaining charge, 5/9 is used for the trip home, leaving the rest. What fraction of the ORIGINAL full charge is left after the trip home?

explanationFigure.alt: Two bars, each cut into 12 equal pieces. The first bar has 10 shaded for 5 sixths, the second bar has 3 shaded for 1 quarter, the two fractions used in this problem.

problems.prompt: A rope is 5/6 of 48 meters long. After tying a knot, 1/4 of that rope's length is used up in the knot. How many meters of usable rope remain?
explanation: Of means times: 5/6 of 48 is the rope's length. Divide 48 by 6 to get 8, times 5 is 40 meters.
The knot uses 1/4 of that 40 meters: divide 40 by 4 to get 10 meters used.
Usable rope left is 40 minus 10, which is 30 meters.
problems.useAgain: when a fraction of an amount is found first, then another fraction of that same result is used up or removed.
hints: Find the rope's actual length first, before worrying about the knot.
Subtract the knot's length from the rope's total length, do not just find a fraction of a fraction.
problems.socraticHint: Is the amount of rope 'left over' the same as 'the fraction not used', or do you need actual meters to answer this question?

variant.prompt: A ribbon is 3/4 of 60 centimeters long. After cutting a bow, 1/3 of that ribbon's length is used up. How many centimeters of usable ribbon remain?

explanationFigure.alt: One bar cut into 5 equal pieces with 4 shaded, showing 4 fifths, the correct fraction: you divide by the bottom number 5 first, not the top number 4.

problems.prompt:
Priya found 4/5 of 40 like this:
Line 1: Of means times, so 4/5 of 40 is 4/5 times 40.
Line 2: Divide by the top number, 4: 40 divided by 4 is 10.
Line 3: Multiply by the bottom number, 5: 10 times 5 is 50.
Line 4: So 4/5 of 40 is 50.
Which line is wrong?
explanation: Line 2 is wrong: to find a fraction of an amount, divide by the bottom number first, not the top number.
Lines 1, 3 and 4 are correct arithmetic once you accept line 2's number, but line 2 starts from the wrong number.
Dividing 40 by the bottom number, 5, gives 8, the value of one fifth.
Multiply 8 by the top number, 4: 8 times 4 is 32, so 4/5 of 40 is really 32.
problems.useAgain: when you find a fraction of an amount and need to divide by the bottom number, not the top.
hints: Of means times, and finding one part first: which number tells you how many equal parts to cut the 40 into?
Check which of the two numbers in 4/5, the top or the bottom, tells you the size of one equal slice.
problems.socraticHint: If you cut 40 into 4 equal slices instead of 5, would each slice be bigger or smaller than it should be?

variant.prompt:
Omar found 3/8 of 24 like this:
Line 1: Of means times, so 3/8 of 24 is 3/8 times 24.
Line 2: Divide by the top number, 3: 24 divided by 3 is 8.
Line 3: Multiply by the bottom number, 8: 8 times 8 is 64.
Line 4: So 3/8 of 24 is 64.
Which line is wrong?

explanationFigure.alt: One bar cut into 6 equal pieces with 5 shaded, showing 5 sixths, the fraction of 30 this problem asks for.

problems.prompt: Which of these equals 5/6 of 30?
explanation: Of means times, so 5/6 of 30 is 5/6 x 30.
Divide 30 by 6 to get 5, the value of one sixth.
Multiply 5 by 5 to get 25, the value of five sixths.
The trap answers come from stopping after the division, or from a small slip in the multiplication.
problems.useAgain: when the top number of the fraction is only one less than the bottom number.
hints: Divide by the bottom number of the fraction first.
Multiply that result by the top number.
problems.socraticHint: The top number of five sixths is only one away from the bottom number. Does that make five sixths of an amount land closer to the whole amount, or closer to half of it?

variant.prompt: Which of these equals 7/10 of 40?

explanationFigure.alt: One bar cut into 8 equal pieces with 3 shaded, showing 3 eighths, the fraction of 32 this problem asks for.

problems.prompt: Which of these equals 3/8 of 32?
explanation: Of means times: 3/8 of 32 is 3/8 x 32.
Divide 32 by 8 to get 4, the value of one eighth.
Multiply 4 by 3 to get 12, the value of three eighths.
The trap answers come from stopping after the division, using the wrong fraction, or subtracting instead of multiplying.
problems.useAgain: when a fraction of an amount is asked for directly.
hints: Divide by the bottom number of the fraction first.
Multiply that result by the top number.
problems.socraticHint: Once you know the value of one eighth of 32, what do you do to it to reach three eighths instead?

variant.prompt: Which of these equals 5/7 of 28?

explanationFigure.alt: Three bars, each cut into 4 equal pieces. The first two bars are fully shaded, and the third bar has 1 of its 4 pieces shaded, showing the mixed number 2 and 1 quarter.

problems.prompt: Which of these equals 2 1/4 lots of 2?
explanation: Of means times: 'lots of' means multiply.
Break the mixed number into a whole part and a fraction part: 2 and 1/4.
Multiply the whole part by 2: 2 x 2 makes 4 in total. Multiply the fraction part by 2: 1/4 x 2 is 2/4, which is 1/2.
Add the two results together: 4 plus 1/2 makes 4 and 1/2 in total. The trap answers come from forgetting to scale the fraction part, or scaling only part of it.
problems.useAgain: when a rate given as a mixed number needs to be scaled up by a whole number of repeats.
hints: Multiply the whole number part and the fraction part separately.
Add the two results back together at the end.
problems.socraticHint: You already scaled a mixed number by 3 in an earlier problem, and this time it is only scaled by 2. What changes about the two separate pieces you multiply, and what stays the same about the method?

variant.prompt: Which of these equals 1 2/3 lots of 3?

explanationFigure.alt: Three bars, each cut into 2 equal pieces. The first two bars are fully shaded, and the third bar has 1 of its 2 pieces shaded, showing the mixed number 2 and 1 half.

problems.prompt: Which is 2 1/2 lots of 6?
explanation: Of means times: 2 1/2 lots of 6 is 2 1/2 x 6.
Multiply the whole part by 6: 2 x 6 is 12.
Multiply the fraction part by 6: 1/2 x 6 is 3.
Add the two results together: 12 plus 3 is 15.
problems.useAgain: when a mixed number multiplied by a whole number is given as a list of choices.
hints: Split the mixed number into its whole part and its fraction part first.
Multiply each part by 6 separately, then add the two results.
problems.socraticHint: Two and a half lots of six is two whole lots plus one half lot. Which two smaller amounts do you need to work out before you add them together?

variant.prompt: Which is 3 1/2 lots of 8?

problems.prompt: 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, ... What is the next number?
explanation: Find the rule: look at what changes from one term to the next.
5 minus 2 is 3 and 8 minus 5 is 3 as well. 11 minus 8 is 3 and 14 minus 11 is 3 as well. Each term adds 3 to the one before.
14 plus 3 is 17.
problems.useAgain: when a row of numbers grows by the same amount every step.
hints: Look at the gap between each pair of neighbouring numbers.
Add that same gap to the last number to find the next one.
problems.socraticHint: Neighbouring numbers in this row are always the same distance apart. Once you have found that distance, what do you do with the very last number in the list?

variant.prompt: 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, ... What is the next number?

problems.prompt: Invent your own knights-and-knaves puzzle, like the ones from week one: knights always tell the truth, knaves always lie. Choose three characters and give each one exactly one statement, so that there is exactly one way to label all three a knight or a knave that makes every statement come out true or false the right way. Write out your three characters and their statements, state the one solution, then prove no other assignment works by checking every other combination and showing each one breaks a rule.
explanation: Start by picking the solution first: decide privately which of your three characters are knights and which are knaves, before writing any statements.

Write a statement for each character that would actually be true if they are the knight you picked. The statement should come out false if they are the knave you picked instead. This is the way if then let you check both cases back in week one.
Check every other way to label the three characters, all seven other combinations. Make sure each one makes at least one statement break its own rule.
If another combination also works, the puzzle has more than one solution, so change a statement and check again.
problems.useAgain: when you want to build your own logic puzzle that has exactly one working answer.
hints: Decide who is a knight and who is a knave in your head first, before writing any statement.
For each character, write a sentence that would be true if they are the knight you picked, or false if they are the knave you picked.
problems.socraticHint: With three characters that can each be a knight or a knave, how many total combinations are there to check before you can be sure only one of them works?

problems.prompt: A row of shapes goes: circle, circle, square, circle, circle, square, circle, circle. What shape comes next?
explanation: Find the rule: circle, circle, square is one small group that keeps repeating.
Count from the start: circle, circle, square, circle, circle, square is two full groups, using all 6 shapes.
The next two shapes, circle, circle, are the start of a third group.
The third shape in every group is always square, so square comes next.
problems.useAgain: when a row of shapes repeats a small group over and over.
hints: Look for a small group of shapes that keeps repeating.
Count how many shapes are in one group, then see how far into the next group the row has gone.
problems.socraticHint: The repeating group of shapes here is three shapes long. Once you know how many shapes have appeared so far in total, how do you figure out where you are inside the next group?

variant.prompt: A row of shapes goes: triangle, triangle, triangle, star, triangle, triangle, triangle, star, triangle, triangle. What shape comes next?

problems.prompt: A function machine turns 2 into 7, turns 4 into 13, and turns 6 into 19. What does it turn 10 into?
explanation: Find the rule: check what happens between the in and out numbers for each pair.
2 to 7: 2 times 3 is 6, plus 1 makes 7 exactly. 4 to 13: 4 times 3 is 12, plus 1 makes 13 exactly. 6 to 19: 6 times 3 is 18, plus 1 makes 19 exactly.
Every pair follows the same two-step rule: times 3, then plus 1.
10 times 3 is 30, plus 1 is 31.
problems.useAgain: when a function machine shows several in and out pairs and you need to find the two-step rule connecting them.
hints: Try figuring out what number to multiply by first, then what to add or subtract.
Check that the same two-step rule works for every pair before you use it on the new number.
problems.socraticHint: This function machine does two things to every number that goes in, not just one. Which operation would you test first, and how would you check it against all three pairs before trusting it?

variant.prompt: A function machine turns 1 into 5, turns 3 into 11, and turns 5 into 17. What does it turn 8 into?

problems.prompt: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ... What is the next number?
explanation: Find the rule: check if these numbers relate to counting numbers in a simple way.
1 is 1 x 1, 4 is 2 x 2, and 9 is 3 x 3 as well. 16 is 4 x 4, and 25 is 5 x 5 as well. Each term is a counting number multiplied by itself.
The next counting number after 5 is 6, and 6 x 6 is 36.
problems.useAgain: when a row of numbers grows faster and faster in a way that matches counting numbers multiplied by themselves.
hints: Try multiplying each position number by itself: 1st by 1st, 2nd by 2nd, and so on.
The pattern is 1x1, 2x2, 3x3, then keep going in that same style.
problems.socraticHint: If 5 times 5 is a 5 by 5 grid of dots, what would the next bigger square grid of dots look like sitting next to it?

variant.prompt: 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, ... What is the next number?

problems.prompt: A function machine turns 3 into 5, turns 6 into 11, and turns 9 into 17. What does it turn 12 into?
explanation: Find the rule: check what happens between the in and out numbers for each pair.
3 to 5: 3 times 2 is 6, minus 1 leaves 5 exactly. 6 to 11: 6 times 2 is 12, minus 1 leaves 11 exactly. 9 to 17: 9 times 2 is 18, minus 1 leaves 17 exactly.
Every pair follows the same two-step rule: times 2, then minus 1.
12 times 2 is 24, minus 1 is 23.
problems.useAgain: when a function machine's rule involves subtracting instead of adding after the multiply step.
hints: Look for a multiply step and then an add or subtract step.
Test your rule on all three pairs before predicting the new one.
problems.socraticHint: Looking at all three given pairs together as one puzzle, does this machine only multiply, or does it do something to the number afterward too?

variant.prompt: A function machine turns 2 into 3, turns 5 into 9, and turns 8 into 15. What does it turn 11 into?

problems.prompt: A sequence starts 2, 4, 8, 16. Marco says the rule is 'add 2 each time', which fits going from 2 to 4. Sara says the rule is 'double each time'. Test both rules against all four numbers. Which rule keeps working for every step, and which one breaks?
options: Marco's rule keeps working, Sara's breaks
Sara's rule keeps working, Marco's breaks
Both rules keep working the whole way
Neither rule works past the first two numbers
explanation: Break the pattern: test a candidate rule against every step, not just the first one, to see if it survives.
Marco's rule, add 2, gives 2, 4, 6, 8 in a row. It matches the first two numbers, but breaks on the third, since the real sequence has 8, not 6.
Sara's rule, double each time, gives 2, 4, 8, 16, which matches every number in the sequence.
Testing against more terms is what breaks the weak rule and confirms the strong one.
problems.useAgain: when two different rules both seem to fit the first couple of terms, and you need to find out which one really survives.
hints: Apply each rule to every number in the sequence, not just the first step.
The rule that survives every single term is the one that keeps working.
problems.socraticHint: You have two rules that both explain the jump from the first number to the second. What happens when you check each rule against the third number instead of stopping early?

variant.prompt: A sequence starts 3, 6, 12, 24. Priya says the rule is 'add 3 each time', which fits going from 3 to 6. Tom says the rule is 'double each time'. Test both rules against all four numbers. Which rule keeps working for every step, and which one breaks?
options: Priya's rule keeps working, Tom's breaks
Tom's rule keeps working, Priya's breaks
Both rules keep working the whole way
Neither rule works past the first two numbers

problems.prompt: Here are three numbers: 2, 4, 6. The obvious rule is 'add 2 each time', which predicts 8 next. Invent a different rule that also fits 2, 4 and 6 perfectly, but gives a different fourth number than 8. Write your rule in words, show that it fits all three numbers, and say what it predicts for the fourth number instead.

mustMention: a fourth number that is different from 8
why more than one rule can fit the same numbers

explanation: Break the pattern: many different rules can fit the same three numbers, not just the simplest one.
One example: add 2 for the first two steps, but add 4 after that. It still gives 2, 4, 6 for the first three numbers, since those steps only ever used the add-2 part.
For the fourth number, this rule says add 4 instead of add 2, so 6 plus 4 is 10, not 8.
This shows the obvious rule, add 2 forever, was only one option among many that fit the first three numbers.
problems.useAgain: when only a few numbers or examples are given and you want to check whether the obvious rule is really the only one that fits.
hints: You do not need a fancy rule. It is fine for your rule to change what it does after the third number.
Check your rule against all three given numbers before you use it to predict the fourth.
problems.socraticHint: A rule does not have to keep doing the same thing forever. What could a rule quietly do differently starting only from the step after the numbers you were given?

steps.title: Explain it
steps.prompt: Pick the hardest problem from Patterns. Write why your answer must be right, one idea per sentence. Name the idea you used.

steps.title: Explain back
steps.prompt: Say out loud how you found the rule, as if to a friend who has never seen this puzzle before.
